cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica) ripe leaf, often gong ting or golden-bud grades
processing: Loose ripe pu-erh is steamed briefly and hand-rolled or moulded into a tight 6–8 g ball, dried and wrapped individually; the material is ordinary shu, often a fine grade chosen because it rolls well.
harvest_season: Rolled from finished ripe tea of any season; sold by production year.
appearance_dry: A tight dark-brown sphere the size of a large marble, often speckled with golden buds, in a paper twist.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, pale in the first steep and deepening as the ball opens.
appearance_wet: The ball softens over three steeps into a mound of fine, dark, relaxed leaf.
taste_profile: Classic ripe sweetness in a slow-release form: dates, cocoa and damp wood, a creamy body once the ball has opened, and a clean, mild finish; fine-grade balls are richer and fade sooner.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water, the second rinse 20–30 seconds, to loosen the ball; or treat the first steep as a long warm-up. One ball per 120–150 ml. Do not pry it open; it will unfurl by the third steep. Perfect for a mug or thermos.

vintage_note: Sold by production year in bags, tins and gift boxes, by count or by weight, and almost always young (1–5 years); the format became common around 2012–2015 and there is no tradition of ageing it, though the tight ball does hold the pile smell a little longer than loose tea, so a year or two of age helps. The year is a freshness date rather than a vintage; what matters is the grade and cleanliness of the shu inside, which the ball hides until you brew it.
description:
Ripe dragon balls are shu pu-erh rolled into single-session spheres of about 7–8 g, and they are the most giftable form of ripe tea: no cake to break, no dust, one ball in a mug or gaiwan and the job is done. They turn up in every tea shop and most Chinese gift boxes, and the better ones are made from fine-grade leaf.

The tea is finished ripe pu-erh, often gong ting or golden-bud grade because small leaf rolls into a neat ball, given a quick steam and rolled tightly by hand or mould, then dried and wrapped in a twist of paper. The compression is high, so the ball opens slowly and keeps its pile smell a little longer than loose tea.

In the cup it tastes like whatever shu went into it, released over three steeps: dates, cocoa and damp wood, a creamy body once it has opened, a clean mild finish. Give it two long boiling rinses or a thirty-second first steep, never pull it apart, and it will run eight or nine infusions; in a thermos it will give a whole afternoon.

They are sold by production year, by count and by weight, and the main variable is the quality of the tea inside, which the ball hides: a clean date-and-wood smell on the dry ball is a good sign, a fishy or sour one is not. Cheap balls are rolled from fragments and dust and brew cloudy; better ones from a named factory or a boutique maker brew clear and sweet. They do not need ageing and are not sold for it.

They are the easiest pu-erh to carry, to gift and to brew at a desk, and a kind introduction to ripe tea for anyone put off by the look of a cake.
